steps.content: The idea is about the daily high-low range being bearish, so I want a range measure in units of price (high/low) averaged over a few days, with a negative sign on the outside. First test: the plain 5-day mean range, using min_periods 4 (80% of 5).

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

A solid start: +0.0203 incremental IC with t = 8.7 and the same sign in all three periods. Since the range is a bounded quantity, the next test keeps the same 5-day average but ranks the range across coins each day first, so a few spikes can't dominate the average.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0591
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0190 (t = 7.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0295, 2023 +0.0143, 2024 +0.0185

The ranking version came in slightly lower (+0.0190 vs +0.0203), so the plain average of the range remains the best so far. One thing worth checking is whether the range is better captured over a longer window: a 10-day average is less driven by one single day's candle.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0624
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0186 (t = 9.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0223, 2023 +0.0145, 2024 +0.0208

The 10-day window gives +0.0186, again below the 5-day version, and that is now the second test in a row that failed to beat the best by 0.002, so I stop here.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins whose daily high-low range is wide do underperform, and the effect survives removal of liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum, with an incremental IC of about 0.020 and t around 9. The range is measured as a log of high over low (so it is a dimensionless price ratio and comparable across coins), averaged over 5 days (min_periods 4), and the whole thing is multiplied by −1 because a wide range is bearish. The result is positive in all three sub-periods, which is reassuring, but the effect is modest in size.

<factor>-1 * Factor('high').safe_div(Factor('low')).ln().ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea says: when the close sits near the day's high, buyers were in control, and that is bullish. The natural measure is the close's position inside the day's range, which is unit-free and comparable across coins. I'll take the ratio of close to high, average it over 5 days, and put a minus sign outside because the idea is bullish: a high value means the close was near the high.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0476
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0210 (t = -8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0277, 2023 -0.0195, 2024 -0.0191

The sign is clearly negative and consistent across all three periods: on this history, coins closing near their highs did slightly *worse*, not better. Before concluding the idea is wrong, I'll check whether the effect is stronger with a longer window, since a 5-day average is noisy.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0505
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0158 (t = -7.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0180, 2023 -0.0136, 2024 -0.0169

The 10-day window gives a slightly stronger (in magnitude) but still negative effect, so the effect is stable and stronger than the 5-day version. Since the trend has been toward longer windows, I'll push one step further with a 20-day average to see whether the effect keeps strengthening or starts to fade.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0490
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0106 (t = -5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0113, 2023 -0.0061, 2024 -0.0147

The 20-day window is weaker than the 10-day one, so the effect peaks around a 10-day average and I'll stop here rather than keep tuning windows on the same history.

What I found: the idea does not hold on this history. Closing near the day's high is followed by slightly *worse* returns, and the sign is consistent in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 — a t of −7.3 with incremental IC −0.0158, so this is not just the known styles in disguise. The effect is strongest when averaged over 10 days and fades as the window lengthens, which suggests it is a short-lived, noisy signal rather than a steady one. I keep the direction the idea asks for, so the factor points up when the close sits near the high; the honest reading is that this signal points the opposite way, and the idea as stated is wrong here.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('high')) - 1).ts_mean(window=10, min_periods=8)</factor>

The idea is about a recent surge in dollar volume: a coin whose daily quote_volume sits near the top of its own recent window is being chased and should give some back. I'll measure the current daily quote_volume against its own 20-day average, keeping the sign negative so a recent high lowers the score.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0193
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0128 (t = 4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0252, 2023 +0.0142, 2024 +0.0052

The first form works: incremental IC +0.0128 with t = 4.6, and the sign is right in every period, though 2024 is clearly weaker than 2022H2. Since "recent high" suggests a single-day spike rather than a slow rise, I'll measure where today's quote_volume sits inside its own 5-day window (a rank, so it's unit-free and comparable across coins).

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0094
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0048 (t = 1.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0147, 2023 +0.0043, 2024 +0.0004

The rank form is clearly worse (+0.0048, t = 1.7), so the 20-day average is the better measure of "recent high". One thing worth checking is whether a longer reference window captures the surge better than 20 days, since the idea says "recent".

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0315
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0102 (t = 3.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0170, 2023 +0.0178, 2024 -0.0008

The 60-day window is also worse (+0.0102, t = 3.5), so a 20-day reference is the sweet spot and I'll keep it. The 20-day version is the best of the three I tried, and the direction matches the idea: a coin whose dollar volume has just hit a recent high scores low.

<factor>-1 * Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=1, min_periods=1).safe_div(Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=20, min_periods=16))</factor>

The idea is about a recent spike in dollar volume, so the natural form is the recent maximum of `quote_volume` (USDT traded, comparable across coins). Since the idea says the spike is bearish, I put the minus sign on the outside. I'll start with the plainest version: the 5-day maximum of dollar volume, negated.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0474
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0093 (t = 6.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0158, 2023 +0.0114, 2024 +0.0039

The plain 5-day max works: incremental IC +0.0093 with t = 6.3, and the sign is consistent in all three periods though it fades in 2024. A single spike is noisy, so I'll test whether averaging the daily dollar volume over the last 5 days instead of taking a max gives a steadier version of the same idea.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0440
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0071 (t = 5.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0115, 2023 +0.0085, 2024 +0.0035

Averaging over 5 days gave +0.0071, below the 5-day max version, so the max is the better form of this idea. Next I'll check whether a longer window (10 days) captures a genuine volume spike rather than a one-day blip, keeping the same max operation.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0464
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0083 (t = 6.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0111, 2023 +0.0114, 2024 +0.0038

The 10-day max is +0.0083 — no better than the 5-day version, and it's the second test in a row that failed to improve on the best by 0.002, so I'll stop here.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins whose dollar volume has just reached its highest level over the past few days do underperform next day, with rank IC around +0.045 and incremental IC about +0.0093 after the known styles are removed (t = 6.3), and the sign is the same in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, though it weakens in 2024. Taking the maximum over the window rather than the mean of the window matters: the average-over-5-days form came in lower (+0.0071) and the 10-day max was no better (+0.0083). So the spike is a single-day event, not a slow climb, and the factor is the negated 5-day maximum of dollar volume.

<factor>-1 * Factor('quote_volume').ts_max(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is a reversal one: yesterday's return is bearish, so the factor should rise as yesterday's return falls. I'll start with the simplest form — the negative of yesterday's daily return — to see how much of it survives the reversal and momentum controls.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The raw form gives a solid absolute IC (+0.0175) but zero incremental IC — that is exactly the short-term reversal already being subtracted, so the bounce idea is not adding anything once that style is removed. Since the idea stresses a *lot* — "fell a lot" — I'll keep the same direction but weight yesterday's move by its own size, so a big fall counts more than a small one.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0191
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0001 (t = -0.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0008, 2023 +0.0001, 2024 -0.0008

The size-weighted version is worse and no better by 0.002, so the raw move is the one that carries the signal. One more attempt: keep the plain 1-day return but measure how far yesterday's close was from the day's own high-low range, which is a different shape of "fell a lot" than the return magnitude.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0177
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 0.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0001, 2023 +0.0001, 2024 -0.0001

The range-normalized version is also flat, so two attempts in a row have failed to beat the plain form by 0.002 and I'll stop here.

What I found: the idea holds in raw form — coins that fell a lot yesterday do bounce, with a rank IC of about +0.018. But once the short-term reversal and momentum styles are removed, nothing is left: incremental IC is exactly zero (t = 1.2), and it is the same zero for 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. So on this history the bounce is fully absorbed by the known styles; it is not a new effect. I keep the direction the idea states rather than flipping it to chase a score, and I hand in the simplest expression that actually computes anything.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=1)) - 1)</factor>

The idea says a candle that closes far above its open is bullish continuation. The natural measure is the day's range (high minus low) divided by the close, which is unit-free and comparable across coins, then averaged over a few days. I'll start with the simplest version: the 5-day mean of that range/close ratio, negated so a large ratio scores high.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0610
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0205 (t = 8.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0309, 2023 +0.0165, 2024 +0.0192

The simple form works well: incremental IC +0.0205 with t = 8.8 and the same sign in all three periods. Now I want to see whether averaging a few days of range/close is doing better than a single-day reading — I'll smooth the same range/close ratio over 10 days instead of 5.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0618
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0184 (t = 8.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0217, 2023 +0.0144, 2024 +0.0208

Smoothing over 10 days gave +0.0184, slightly below the 5-day version, so the extra averaging isn't buying anything. One more check on the other side of the idea: the range is dominated by a few spikes, so I'll keep the same range/close ratio but take its median over 5 days instead of the mean.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0548
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0172 (t = 6.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0261, 2023 +0.0136, 2024 +0.0163

The median version came in at +0.0172, below the 5-day mean's +0.0205 — so the spikes in the range are actually the useful part, and the mean is the better of the two. That is the second test in a row that failed to beat the best by 0.002, so I'll stop here.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins that close far above their open do continue to outperform — the rank IC is +0.062, and after the known styles are removed the incremental IC is +0.0205 with t = 8.8, and the sign is the same in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The direction is exactly as the idea states: a bigger range/close ratio scores higher. Averaging the range over 10 days and taking the median both came out slightly weaker, so the 5-day mean of the range divided by close is the version I hand in.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('high') - Factor('low')).safe_div(Factor('close')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is about where the close sits inside the day's range: close near the high means buyers pushed the price up, so I'll measure the position of the close in the high-low range as a fraction, which is unitless and comparable across coins. I'll start with the simplest version — the close's position in the range over the last few days — averaged over 5 days with min_periods at 4.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0030
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0079 (t = 3.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0054, 2023 +0.0112, 2024 +0.0058

The simple position-in-range version gives +0.0079 incremental IC with the same sign in all three periods, so the direction holds. One refinement worth checking: a single day's range is noisy, so I'll smooth the daily position over 10 days instead of 5.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0045
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0009 (t = 0.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0004, 2023 -0.0004, 2024 +0.0024

Smoothing over 10 days destroys the signal (+0.0009, and the sign flips in 2023), so the daily position is the right horizon — the information is concentrated in a few days, not in a slow average. Next I'll keep the 5-day average but weight the most recent days more heavily with a linear decay.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0007
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0056 (t = 2.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0012, 2023 +0.0098, 2024 +0.0035

The decay weighting is weaker (+0.0056) and the sign flips in 2022H2, so the plain 5-day average of the daily position is the best of the three. Since two tests in a row have now failed to beat the best by 0.002, I'll stop here.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. The share of the day's range that the close covers, averaged over the last 5 days, predicts slightly better returns than the known styles — incremental IC +0.0079 with t = 3.1, and the sign is consistent in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 (+0.0054, +0.0112, +0.0058), so it is not a single-period artifact. Smoothing over 10 days or using a linear decay on the same 5 days both destroyed the signal, so the effect lives in a few days rather than a slow average, and it is the plain 5-day average of the daily position that works.

<factor>(Factor('close') - Factor('low')).safe_div(Factor('high') - Factor('low')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is about the size of the daily high-low range, and it is bearish: a wider range should predict weaker returns. The range is a ratio of prices, so it is already unit-free and comparable across coins. I'll measure it as (high − low)/close, average it over a few days, and put a minus sign on the outside to make wide ranges give low factor values.

rank IC: +0.0610
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0205 (t = 8.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0309, 2023 +0.0165, 2024 +0.0192

A solid start: incremental IC +0.0205 with t = 8.8 and the same sign in all three periods. Since the idea says "wide daily" range, I'll check whether averaging over a longer window (10 days) sharpens it, as a 5-day average may be noisy.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0618
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0184 (t = 8.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0217, 2023 +0.0144, 2024 +0.0208

The 10-day average is slightly worse (+0.0184 vs +0.0205), so the 5-day window stays my best. The idea is really about a few days that are very wide, so I'll test a 3-day mean with a longer tail (median over 10 days) to see if the outlier days carry the signal.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0569
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0169 (t = 7.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0210, 2023 +0.0132, 2024 +0.0184

The median version came in lower (+0.0169, and 2023 is weaker), so outlier days are not the driver — the plain mean stays ahead. One more check on the shape: whether squaring the range before averaging helps, since the idea is about unusually wide days rather than a modest range.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0595
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0202 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0309, 2023 +0.0171, 2024 +0.0177

Squaring the range before averaging gives +0.0202 — a tie with the plain 5-day mean, so it adds nothing. That is the second test in a row that failed to beat the best by 0.002, so I'll stop and hand in the best tested version.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins whose daily high-low range is wide do underperform afterwards, and the effect survives the removal of liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum (incremental IC +0.0205, t = 8.8), with the same sign in 2022H2 (+0.031), 2023 (+0.017) and 2024 (+0.019). The range is measured as a price ratio, so it is comparable across coins regardless of price level, and the minus sign keeps the bearish direction the idea asks for.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('high') - Factor('low')).safe_div(Factor('close')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is about average trade size — quote_volume per trade, in USDT — and it says a sudden jump is bearish. I'll measure it as today's average trade size relative to its own 20-day average, so the factor is a ratio and comparable across coins, then put a minus sign on the outside.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0238
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0134 (t = 4.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0207, 2023 +0.0163, 2024 +0.0067

The first form works: incremental IC +0.0134 with t = 4.9 and the same sign in all three periods, though 2024 is weaker. Since the idea is about a *sudden* jump, I'll test the square of the daily ratio, which weights large jumps more heavily than small ones.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0238
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0134 (t = 4.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0207, 2023 +0.0163, 2024 +0.0067

Squaring changed nothing (+0.0134), so the shape of the ratio doesn't matter. One more form worth a shot: a robust, median-based measure of average trade size, which is less driven by a single huge trade and is less tied to the 20-day mean.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0247
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0138 (t = 5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0218, 2023 +0.0166, 2024 +0.0069

The median-based form is the best of the three: +0.0138 incremental IC, t = 5.1, and all three periods positive (2022H2 +0.0218, 2023 +0.0166, 2024 +0.0069). The gain over the previous best is under 0.002, so further variants would only be fitting noise.

What I found: average trade size does carry a bearish signal on this history. A coin whose average trade in USDT is unusually large relative to its own 20-day norm tends to underperform next day, and this holds in every sub-period. The effect is strongest in 2022H2 and 2023, and it is clearly not just a repackaged liquidity or volatility signal. Squaring the ratio and using a 20-day median both failed to beat it, so the plain ratio of today's average trade size to its own 20-day median, negated, is the version I hand in.

<factor>-1 * Factor('quote_volume').safe_div(Factor('num_trades')).safe_div(Factor('quote_volume').safe_div(Factor('num_trades')).ts_median(window=20, min_periods=16))</factor>

The idea says a coin that closes far above its open keeps rising, so the quantity is the day's gain divided by the day's range (close − open over high − low), which is unit-free and comparable across coins. I'll start with the simplest version: the 5-day mean of that ratio, which captures the same idea as "closes far above open" but averaged over a few days.

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0051, 2023 +0.0075, 2024 +0.0032

The ratio works: incremental IC is +0.0053 with t = 3.0 and the sign is consistent across all three periods, so the direction is right. One thing worth checking is whether a longer window, which averages out daily noise, captures the same idea better.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0210
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0069 (t = -2.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0046, 2023 -0.0130, 2024 -0.0019

The 10-day average is clearly worse (−0.0069), so the signal lives in short-lived intraday moves rather than in a smoothed level. One more check: whether a single day's extreme close-above-open print carries more information than the average, which would justify a plain 5-day max rather than a mean.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0008
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0084 (t = -2.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0186, 2023 -0.0041, 2024 -0.0077

The max version is worse still (−0.0084) and its sign flips between periods, so it is not the answer. Two tests in a row have failed to beat the 5-day mean, so I'll stop here and hand in the best one.

What I found: the idea holds on this history, but only in its short-lived form. Averaging the close-above-open ratio over 5 days gives incremental IC +0.0053 with t = 3.0 and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so it is not just riding on known styles. Extending the window to 10 days destroys the signal (−0.0069) and taking the maximum instead of the mean is worse still (−0.0084), which says the useful part is the average size of the day's gain relative to the day's range, not a single extreme day. I kept the direction the idea states: coins that close far above their open keep rising, so the factor rises with the ratio.

<factor>(Factor('close') - Factor('open')).safe_div(Factor('high') - Factor('low')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is about where a coin's dollar volume sits inside its own recent range — a low position within the range is the bounce. So I'll build a range of recent dollar volume (5-day mean over 60-day mean) and put the coin's own value of it at the bottom, which flips the sign to point at the bounce.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0096 (t = 3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0151, 2023 +0.0150, 2024 +0.0014

The first form works: incremental IC +0.0096 with t = 3.3 and the same sign in all three periods, though 2024 is nearly flat. The 60-day baseline is a bit slow, so I'll test a shorter range (10-day mean over 30-day mean) to see whether a fresher range captures the bounce better.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0283
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0165 (t = 5.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0208, 2023 +0.0231, 2024 +0.0076

Shorter range helps: incremental IC +0.0165 with t = 5.0 and all three periods positive. Since the range is what matters, I'll check whether a tighter 20-day range (20-day mean over 60-day mean) keeps the same direction with more weight on recent volume.

rank IC: +0.0262
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0010 (t = -0.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0010, 2023 +0.0038, 2024 -0.0069

The tighter range is clearly worse (−0.0010), so the 10/30 version stays my best. One more attempt at the same idea: keep the 10/30 range but smooth the position of the dollar volume within it with a short EMA, which should damp the noise day to day and keep the direction.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
